question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

8.text:
In CFOP the U–face is already in place after OLL so the nine U-stickers carry
no information at all at all.  What is left is the permutation of the
eight U–layer cubies

* 4 U–edges, each of them is uniquely identified by the single side sticker
that it shows on F/B/L/R,
* 4 U–corners, each of them is uniquely identified by the two side stickers
that it shows on F/B/L/R.

Hence up to rotation the U–layer is completely described by the side
colours of its eight cubies.  In the ordinary visual sense that is eight
different side–sticker positions to be inspected, four edge side stickers
UF,UR,UB,UL and one side sticker for each of the four corners, i.e. the
12 sticker faces 4×1+4×2 which belong to the U–layer on the four side
faces.  In the information–theoretic sense the eighth cubie is forced by
the even parity of a 3×3 permutation so that seven independent side
sticker inspections suffice to pin down the 21 PLL permutations, the
familiar “seven-sticker” minimum, eight sticker positions in the usual
practical description.  This is the eight side stickers of the U-layer
that are normally spoken of as the four edge stickers + the four corner
side stickers that have to be read off the U-layer.  Up to parity that is
seven independent non-U stickers; the twelve physical sticker faces of the
U-layer are 4 edge + 8 corner side stickers.

4.text:
In CFOP the OLL step has already made the U face monochromatic.
The only thing that is left to distinguish is the permutation of the
8 cubies that sit on the U layer

* 4 U edges, each of them has one side colour which is visible on the
F,R,B,L faces, and
* 4 U corners, each of them has two side colours which are visible on
the F,R,B,L faces.

The side colour of a U edge and the side colour of a U corner is the
only thing that makes the cubie distinguishable, because the U sticker
of every U cubie is the same.  In the U slice there are therefore

* 4 edge side stickers
* 4×2 = 8 corner side stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers in total, 8 distinct side stickers which are
enough to name the eight U cubies.  Up to a rotation of the whole cube
the eight distinct side stickers can be read from the two faces that
you are actually looking at. In the normal front-right view that is

* F top row : FL-front, F-front, FR-front
* R top row : FR-right, R-right, BR-right

six side stickers of the U layer, the three stickers on the front top
row and the three stickers on the right top row.  It is those six
visible side stickers, i.e. the eight distinct U-layer side stickers,
that carry the information of the 21 PLL classes; the twelve
side stickers of the U slice are the whole set of non-U information
that the last layer contains.  This is usually quoted as the
“six sticker’’ or, in distinct cubie terms, the eight side sticker
PLL recognition.

2.text:
After OLL the whole U face is one colour.  Up to rotation the U face
carries no information about the permutation of the last layer at all.
What remains to be recognised in PLL is the relative disposition of the
four U edges and of the four U corners and the U face itself is
monochrome.  

On the U layer there are

* 4 U–edges, each of which is identified by the one side sticker that
is not on U, and
* 4 U–corners, each of which is identified by the two side stickers
that are not on U.

That is 4+2×4 = 12 non-U stickers on the U layer, 4 edge stickers and 8
corner stickers.  In the usual AUF convention the whole permutation is
read off the ring of side colours round the U layer.  Up to the cube
rotation the parity of the corner permutation is the parity of the edge
permutation so that in the ordinary speed–cubing sense the case is
normally spoken of as being read off the four edge identifiers, i.e.
four non-U stickers, eight distinct piece identifiers, the 12 side
stickers of the U layer in the completely conservative count.  With a
good AUF you can in practice recognise any of the 21 PLL patterns from
about four to six of those side stickers, the four U–edge stickers being
the usual textbook minimum.  In particular the U face itself gives no
information at all about the PLL case.

10.text:
In CFOP the U–face is already solved after OLL so the U–stickers carry no
permutation information at all.  The permutation of the last layer is the
permutation of the eight U–layer pieces

* 4 U–layer edges.  Each U–edge is completely identified by its single
non–U side sticker. There are 4 of them on the U–layer.
* 4 U–layer corners.  Each U–corner is oriented, the U–sticker is white,
so the piece is identified by its two side stickers.  There are 2×4 = 8
non–U side stickers on the four U–corners.

Hence the U–layer carries

* 4 edge side stickers
* 8 corner side stickers

i.e. 12 physical stickers which are not on the U face, the 12 stickers
that belong to the U–layer but lie on the four side faces.  That is the
information content of a PLL.  Up to the four rotations of the U face the
information can be expressed by the 4 edge side stickers and one
distinguishing side sticker for each of the 4 corners, the 8
effectively distinct non–U observations which are normally quoted for
practical PLL recognition.  The 12 stickers are the 4×1+4×2 stickers of
the U–layer that have to be known in order to know exactly which of the
21 essentially different edge/corner permutations you have.

6.text:
After an OLL the U–layer is orientation solved.  In the usual
convention the centre of the U–face is the colour that is now uniform on
the whole U–face

* U–face = White
* the eight pieces that are on the U–layer are the eight pieces that
belonged to the U–layer in the solved cube

so that the nine up–stickers are now all the same colour and carry no
permutation information at all.  The permutation information of a PLL
is carried entirely by the side stickers of the eight U–pieces.

A U–edge is identified by its one side sticker and a U–corner is
identified by the unordered pair of its two side stickers.  Hence in the
information–theoretic sense the U–layer carries

* 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 8 corner side stickers
* 4 edges   × 1 side sticker  = 4 edge side stickers

i.e. 12 non–U stickers in all, the twelve stickers that are on the
four lateral faces of the top layer.  One identifying sticker per piece
is enough for recognition, i.e. one sticker for each of the eight U
pieces, four corner–identifying stickers and four edge–identifying
stickers.  In practice the six stickers that are visible on the front
and right top rows,

3 front top–row stickers + 3 right top–row stickers,

are enough to recognise the 21 PLL classes up to U–rotation, and with
a single U–rotation you can see the other six side stickers.  This is
the reason why PLL is normally talked about as “the eight U–pieces’’,
four corners and four edges, eight distinct side stickers, i.e. the
twelve side stickers of the U–layer. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

For a PLL the U face is already orientated so all 8 U stickers are the same colour and carry no information. The permutation is carried by the identities of the four U edges and the four U corners. 

One identifying sticker on the side of each piece is enough to tell which piece is in which U slot, and the side sticker is by definition non-U. That is one side sticker per U edge, four in total, and one side sticker per U corner, four in total. In practice you normally look at the four side stickers of the top edges and the four side stickers of the top corners that are visible on the front/right/back/left faces. Once those eight non-top stickers are known the whole permutation of the last layer is fixed and the PLL case is uniquely determined.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the top stickers carry no permutation information at all. You have to read the last layer from the sides. The four U-layer corners are each identifiable by the two side stickers that are visible on the front/side faces of the cube, and the four U-layer edges are identifiable by the single side sticker that sits just below the U sticker. In practice the permutation is over-determined, but the minimal distinguishing set that guarantees a unique PLL is the eight side stickers you can read on the four corners of the U layer. With those eight non-U stickers you can see the cycle structure of the corners and, because the parity of the last layer is fixed, the edge permutation is then forced. Four edges by themselves are not enough to break the mirror/ambiguous cases, so you need the full corner information, i.e. eight non-top-facing stickers, to pin down the PLL case unambiguously in CFOP.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the U stickers give no identifying information. The PLL is a permutation of the 8 cubies that sit on the U layer. An edge cubie is uniquely identified by its single side sticker because the U colour is already known to be the solved top colour, so 1 non-top sticker per edge is needed, 4 in total.

A corner cubie is identified by the pair of side colours. In practice one side colour per corner is enough to tell the four U corners apart in the moment of recognition, the second side colour being implied by the position relative to the other three corners. That is one non-top sticker per corner, 4 in total.

4 edge stickers + 4 corner stickers = 8 non-top-facing stickers are the side information that has to be available to be able to name the permutation unambiguously. With fewer than that two different PLL permutations can share the same visible side colours.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is solved so the whole PLL distinction lives in how the four U-layer corners and four U-layer edges are permuted. The U-face stickers alone give you the top colour pattern, but they do not tell you which physical piece is sitting in each slot – you need the side colour information to resolve the piece identity and hence the permutation.

In practice you can read the permutation from the front-facing side of the last layer: one side sticker per U-layer corner, four stickers, and one side sticker per U-layer edge, four stickers. That is 4+4 = 8 non-U stickers. With the four corner side stickers you can distinguish the corner cycle type and with the four edge side stickers you can distinguish the edge cycle type, and together the corner+edge information is enough to uniquely pick out one of the 21 PLL cases in CFOP recognition. Seeing fewer than that leaves a genuine ambiguity between mirror or cycle-equivalent cases.

9.text:
In CFOP the U face is already colour uniform after OLL. The U stickers
themselves therefore carry no information about the permutation that has
to be done.  All the information that distinguishes the 21 PLL classes
is carried by the side colours of the U layer.

The U layer is

* 4 U edges : 1 non U sticker per edge,
* 4 U corners : 2 non U stickers per corner.

so that there are 4+8 = 12 non-U stickers on the U layer.  Up to a global
rotation of the cube the case is the permutation of the 8 U cubies.  One
cubie is fixed by parity, so information-theoretically 7 distinct
non-U side stickers are enough to fix the permutation and in the usual
``one sticker per cubie'' counting you need one side sticker for each of
the 4 U edges and one side sticker for each of the 4 U corners,

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct U-side
stickers,

i.e. the 12 U-side stickers, 4 edges ×1 and 4 corners ×2, of the last
layer.  This is the side information that is normally inspected for
PLL recognition; the U face itself can be ignored.  Counting both
corner side stickers the U layer contributes 12 non-U stickers, the
8-cubie information being the 4 edge stickers + 4 corner stickers
commonly quoted as eight.  With parity one of the eight may be inferred,
so seven distinct non-U side stickers are information theoretically
necessary and sufficient.

3.text:
In the CFOP last layer the U face is already oriented. The only thing
that is still unknown is which U piece is in which U place.  An U edge
is completely determined by the one side sticker that it shows on the
$D$-side of the U ring and a U corner is completely determined by the
two side stickers that it shows on the $D$–side of the U ring.  In the
usual  top view you therefore have to be able to read the four $U$ edge
pieces

* $U\!F$, $U\!R$, $U\!B$, $U\!L$

by their one side sticker and the four $U$ corner pieces

* $U\!FR$, $U\!RL$, $U\!BL$, $U\!LF$

by one side sticker per corner.  That is the eight U pieces of the
last layer, i.e. four edge stickers and four corner stickers, in
ordinary language “the four edges and the four corners’’ of the U ring.
The whole U ring is 4 edges$\times 1+4$ corners$\times 2=12$ non–U
stickers, 8 of which are information bearing in the sense of one
sticker per piece.

Modulo the usual parity relation of a legal Rubik position the eighth
piece is forced by the other seven, so that seven independent non-$U$
stickers are information–theoretically enough to separate the 21 PLL
classes, the eighth being the familiar parity redundancy.  This is
the statement that is usually quoted as “you need the four edges and
the four corners’’ of the U layer, i.e. eight side stickers of the U
ring, twelve stickers in total on the U ring, seven of which are
independent.  The 8–piece, 12–sticker description is the one used in
practice.

11.text:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented.  All of the U stickers are the
same colour so the U face itself carries no information about the
permutation. The permutation is carried by the side colour(s) of the
eight U pieces.

On the U slice there are

* 4 U edges, 1 side sticker per edge, and
* 4 U corners, 2 side stickers per corner,

i.e. 4+8 = 12 non-U stickers belonging to the U layer.  Those 12 are
the U ring

```
F U R U B U L U
```

which is what you are actually reading when you do a PLL recognition.
Up to rotation the 21 PLL classes are distinguished by the pattern
of those 12 side stickers.  In particular the 4 edges are distinguished
by their one visible side sticker and the 4 corners by their two side
stickers.  Up to the obvious parity of the U layer the last piece of the
8 is forced by the seven others, so in the information theoretic sense
the 21 cases can be disambiguated from 7 distinct non-U stickers of the
U layer, the usual teaching form of which is the 4 edge stickers + the
4 corner identifiers, i.e. 8 distinct piece identifiers, 12 stickers
in the complete U ring.  This is the 12-sticker U ring that is normally
quoted as the PLL reading.  The 7-sticker bound is the usual
“seven is enough” form of the same statement.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is solved so the nine U stickers carry zero permutation information. What remains is the identity of the eight U-layer pieces: four U edges and four U corners. 

An edge is distinguished by its single side sticker, so you need the four edge stickers UF, UR, UB, UL. A corner is distinguished by its two side colours, and in practice you need to be able to read at least one side colour per corner to know which corner sits in which slot, i.e. four corner identifiers. The six stickers you see on the front top row plus the right top row are the convenient glance view, but they do not give you a guaranteed identifier for every one of the eight U pieces at once. The UL edge sticker, the UB edge sticker and the back/left corner information are not in that view, so U-permutations that are mirrors of each other can look identical on that six-sticker window. Once you can read one side sticker for each of the four U edges and one side sticker for each of the four U corners the cycle type of corners and edges is fixed and the PLL case is uniquely determined, up to AUF. That is the eight non-top identifiers that are normally quoted for PLL recognition, the twelve physical non-U stickers on the U ring being the full physical complement.

After OLL the U face is solved so the nine U stickers carry zero permutation information. What remains is the identity of the eight U-layer pieces: four U edges and four U corners. 

An edge is distinguished by its single side sticker, so you need the four edge stickers UF, UR, UB, UL. A corner is distinguished by its two side colours, and in practice you need to be able to read at least one side colour per corner to know which corner sits in which slot, i.e. four corner identifiers. That is 4 + 4 = 8 non-U stickers that have to be available to name the permutation unambiguously.

The six stickers you see on the front top row plus the right top row are the convenient glance view, but they do not give you a guaranteed identifier for every one of the eight U pieces at once. The UL edge sticker, the UB edge sticker and the back/left corner information are not in that view, so U-permutations that are mirrors of each other can look identical on that six-sticker window. Once you can read one side sticker for each of the four U edges and one side sticker for each of the four U corners the cycle type of corners and edges is fixed and the PLL case is uniquely determined, up to AUF. That is the eight non-top identifiers that are normally quoted for PLL recognition, the twelve physical non-U stickers on the U ring being the full physical complement.

I’m landing on eight non-U stickers as the minimal unambiguous set for CFOP PLL recognition.

After OLL the U face is monochrome, so no permutation information lives on the top. What you have to read is the identities of the eight U-layer pieces. An U-edge is identified by its single side sticker, 4 of them. An U-corner is identified by its two side stickers, but for piece identity you need at least one distinguishing side sticker per corner, 4 of them. That is 4 edge stickers + 4 corner stickers = 8 distinct non-top-facing observations that name the eight U cubies.

The 12 stickers of the U-ring, 4×1 edge + 4×2 corner, are the physical total belonging to the U layer. Up to U rotation you can’t get all 12 at once, and you don’t need to. What you do need is one identifier per piece. Seven independent stickers is enough information-theoretically because of parity, but “must be seen” is a worst-case recognition requirement, not an information-theoretic bound.

The six-sticker front-right top-row quote is the number you can see at one instant with a good AUF, 3 front top row + 3 right top row. Mirror and cycle-equivalent PLLs such as U-perm vs Z-perm variants, or the various T/J/Y forms, stay ambiguous until you have a side sticker for each of the four corners and each of the four edges. In practice cubers rotate the cube and read the eight distinct side identifiers, four edges and four corners, which is why PLL is taught as the eight U pieces.

So the conservative, guaranteed-recognition count is eight non-top-facing stickers; twelve is the full U-ring size, seven is the information-theoretic lower bound.

colour for PLL purposes and the PLL is the permutation of the eight
U-layer cubies.

* U edges: 4 edges, 1 side sticker per edge on F/R/B/L. 4 non-U edge stickers.
* U corners: 4 corners, 2 side stickers per corner on F/R/B/L. 8 non-U corner
  stickers.

Physically the U ring

F U R U B U L U

is

4 U edges × 1 side + 4 U corners × 2 sides = 4 + 8 = 12 non-U sticker faces
belonging to the U layer on F,R,B,L. That is the complete physical
information content of a PLL.

For naming the pieces the U colour is already known and the pieces are
oriented after OLL, so one side observation per U piece is enough.

* an U edge is named by its single side sticker : 4 edge identifiers
* an U corner is named in place by one distinguishing side sticker : 4
  corner identifiers

4 edge identifiers + 4 corner identifiers = 8 distinct non-U observations
that name the eight U pieces unambiguously. Those 8 distinct observations
are realised by the 12 physical side stickers of the U ring.

Modulo the even parity of a legal last layer the eighth U cubie is forced
by the other seven, so information theoretically 7 independent non-U side
stickers are enough to separate the 21 essentially different PLL classes.

practical distinct identifiers / 12 physical U-ring stickers.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is permutation inert. The nine U stickers carry no PLL information and the PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies, four U-edges and four U-corners.

Naming a U piece needs a side observation because the U colour is already known and the layer is oriented. 

* a U-edge is named by its single side sticker on F/R/B/L: 4 edge identifiers
* a U-corner is named in place by a distinguishing side sticker on F/R/B/L: 4 corner identifiers

One identifier per U piece is enough to name the eight pieces unambiguously, 4+4 = 8 distinct non-top-facing observations. Those eight identifiers are realised by the 12 physical non-U faces of the U ring F U R U B U L U, 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers.

The six-sticker front top row + right top row glance that is quoted for speed is a real in-hand AUF shortcut, not a guarantee. On a fixed view those six stickers are the three front top stickers and three right top stickers. The UB edge side sticker and the back-left U corner information are completely hidden on that fixed view, and the UL edge side sticker is also not reliably readable without moving the cube.

That is why mirror / cycle-equivalent families remain ambiguous on a six-sticker window: U-perm vs its mirror, the Z-perm variants, and the T/J/Y family all stay indistinguishable until you have a side identifier for each of the four U edges and each of the four U corners. You cannot name the back-left U edge and the back-left U corner from the front-right six stickers alone.

If “must be seen” is taken as worst-case guaranteed identification without assuming you can first choose an optimal AUF and then re-inspect, you need a distinguishing side sticker for each of the four U edges and one distinguishing side sticker for each of the four U corners that you can actually read at the moment of recognition. That is the eight non-top-facing piece identifiers that are normally taught as the safe, AUF-independent PLL reading, the twelve physical U-ring stickers being the over-determined realisation of those eight identifiers. The six-sticker view is best-case after an optimal AUF, not the guaranteed minimum.

6.text:
After OLL the U face is permutation inert. The nine U stickers carry no
PLL information and the last layer is the permutation of the eight
U-layer cubies.

On the U slice

* 4 U edges : 1 side sticker per edge on F/R/B/L
* 4 U corners : 2 side stickers per corner on F/R/B/L

F U R U B U L U

is therefore physically

4 × 1 + 4 × 2 = 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12

With the U colour known and the layer oriented after OLL one side
observation per U piece is enough to name the piece.  An U edge is named
by its single side sticker, 4 edge identifiers, and an U corner can be
named in place by one distinguishing side sticker, 4 corner identifiers,
the second side sticker per corner being the redundancy that makes the
U ring over-determined.

4 edge-identifying non-U stickers + 4 corner-identifying non-U stickers
= 8 distinct non-U observations

for the eight U cubies. Those eight distinct observations are the 12
physical side faces of the U ring, 4×1 edge + 4×2 corner. Modulo the even
parity of a legal last layer the eighth U cubie is forced by the other
seven so information-theoretically 7 independent non-U side stickers are
enough to separate the 21 essentially different PLL classes, the familiar
7 independent / 8 practical distinct identifier / 12 physical sticker
statement.

safe unambiguous reading is the eight piece identifiers, i.e. the twelve
physical non-U stickers of the U ring. The six-sticker front top row +
right top row glance is the familiar in-hand AUF shortcut of that set

view.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is information inert for PLL. The whole last layer is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies, four U-edges and four U-corners, and that permutation lives entirely in the side stickers of those eight cubies.

A U-edge is oriented after OLL so its U colour is known. Its identity is carried by its single side sticker on F/R/B/L.
A U-corner is oriented after OLL so its U colour is known. Its identity in place is carried by a distinguishing side sticker on F/R/B/L; the second side sticker is the redundancy that makes the U ring over-determined.

Hence in naming terms you need one non-U observation per U piece:
4 edge identifiers + 4 corner identifiers = 8 distinct non-top-facing observations.

That is the physical realisation of the U ring
F U R U B U L U
which is 4 edges × 1 side sticker + 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 12 physical non-U sticker faces on F,R,B,L.

The six-sticker front top row + right top row glance that is quoted in speedcubing is real and useful in hand. After an optimal AUF you can see three front top stickers and three right top stickers at once, i.e. six stickers simultaneously. With a subsequent U rotation the other six side stickers of the U ring become visible. That is a best-case AUF shortcut, not a guarantee.

If the requirement is “must be seen” for a guaranteed, AUF-independent identification, you cannot assume the cube will present you with the optimal AUF first and you cannot assume you will be allowed to rotate and re-inspect. The safe, worst-case guaranteed recognition set that is normally taught for CFOP is therefore the eight distinct non-top piece identifiers, four edge side stickers and four corner side stickers, i.e. the twelve physical non-U stickers of the U ring. A U-corner is oriented after OLL so its U colour is known. Its identity in place is carried by a distinguishing side sticker on F/R/B/L; the second side sticker is the redundancy that makes the U ring over-determined.

Hence in naming terms you need one non-U observation per U piece:
4 edge identifiers + 4 corner identifiers = 8 distinct non-top-facing observations.

That is the physical realisation of the U ring
F U R U B U L U
which is 4 edges × 1 side sticker + 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 12 physical non-U sticker faces on F,R,B,L.

The six-sticker front top row + right top row glance that is quoted in speedcubing is real and useful in hand. After an optimal AUF you can see three front top stickers and three right top stickers at once, i.e. six stickers simultaneously. With a subsequent U rotation the other six side stickers of the U ring become visible. That is a best-case AUF shortcut, not a guarantee.

If the requirement is “must be seen” for a guaranteed, AUF-independent identification, you cannot assume the cube will present you with the optimal AUF first and you cannot assume you will be allowed to rotate and re-inspect. On a fixed view the six-sticker window leaves the back-left U edge and the back-left U corner without a reliable side identifier. Mirror and cycle-equivalent families such as U-perm vs its mirror, Z-perm variants and the T/J/Y family remain ambiguous on that six-sticker window until a side identifier for each of the four edges and each of the four corners is available.

The safe, worst-case guaranteed recognition set that is normally taught for CFOP is therefore the eight distinct non-top piece identifiers, four edge side stickers and four corner side stickers, i.e. the twelve physical non-U stickers of the U ring. Seven is the information-theoretic parity bound, twelve is the physical size of the U ring, eight is the practical guaranteed recognition count.

7.text:

A U edge is named by its single side sticker on F/R/B/L. That's 4 edge identifiers.
A U corner is named in place by one distinguishing side sticker on F/R/B/L; the second side sticker per corner is redundancy that makes the U ring over-determined. That's 4 corner identifiers.

4 edge identifiers + 4 corner identifiers = 8 distinct non-top-facing observations that name the eight U pieces unambiguously. Those 8 distinct identifiers are realised physically by the 12 non-U faces of the U ring F U R U B U L U, 4×1 edge + 4×2 corner.

Seven is the information-theoretic parity bound, twelve is the physical size of the U ring, eight is the guaranteed recognition requirement.

After OLL the U face is permutation inert. The nine U stickers carry no PLL
information. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies and that
permutation lives entirely in the side stickers of those eight cubies, the
U ring

F U R U B U L U

* 4 U edges : 1 non-U side sticker per edge on F/R/B/L = 4 edge side stickers
* 4 U corners : 2 non-U side stickers per corner on F/R/B/L = 8 corner side stickers

observation per U piece is enough to name the piece in place.

* a U corner is named in place by one distinguishing side sticker : 4 corner identifiers

realised by the 12 physical side stickers of the U ring, 4×1 edge + 4×2 corner.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is information inert for PLL, so all the PLL information lives in the side stickers of the eight U-layer cubies on the U ring F U R U B U L U. Physically that's 4 U edges ×1 side sticker + 4 U corners ×2 side stickers = 12 non-U sticker faces on F,R,B,L. The nine U stickers carry no permutation information.

For naming the permutation you need one distinguishing side observation per U piece because the U colour and the orientation after OLL are already known. An U edge is named by its single side sticker, 4 edge identifiers. An U corner can be named in place by one distinguishing side sticker, the second side sticker per corner being redundancy. That's 4 edge identifiers + 4 corner identifiers = 8 distinct non-top-facing observations that name the eight U pieces unambiguously.

The familiar six-sticker front top row + right top row glance is real and useful in hand. After an optimal AUF you can see three front top stickers and three right top stickers at once.
